# Review Packet: Forces, Equilibrium and Linear Motion (Chapters 2-3)

Oct 16, 2026

## How to use this packet

This packet walks you through Chapters 2 and 3 in the order the ideas build on each other. Every part has a short explanation, a worked example, and practice questions, and the answer key is at the end.

Chapter 2 asks: **what makes motion change?** The answer is net force. Chapter 3 asks: **how do we describe motion changing?** The answer is velocity, acceleration, graphs, and a few equations. The two chapters connect in one chain:

$$
\text{net force} = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \text{velocity does not change} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \text{acceleration} = 0
$$

Keep that chain in mind. It comes back in almost every part.

**How to work through it**

- Read the **Big idea** first, then follow the **Worked example** with a pencil in your hand.
- Try the practice questions before you look at the answers. A wrong attempt that you then fix teaches more than reading a right answer.
- Show your work and write units: N, m, s, m/s, m/s².
- Use g = 10 m/s² for falling objects unless a question says otherwise.
- Questions marked ★ are challenges. Skip them on a first pass if you are short on time.

## Reference sheet: formulas and when to use them

Every formula you need for Chapters 2 and 3 is in the tables below, along with the situation that tells you to use it. Look here whenever you are not sure where to start.

**Forces (Chapter 2)**

| Tool | What it says | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Net force on a line | Add forces in the same direction; subtract forces in opposite directions. Call right/up positive, left/down negative. | Several forces push or pull along the same line and you want the total. |
| Equilibrium: ΣF = 0 | Net force is zero. The object is at rest (static) or moving at constant velocity (dynamic). | You are told an object is at rest or at constant velocity, or you need an unknown force. |
| Weight: W = m × g | Weight in newtons = mass in kg × 10 N/kg (on Earth). | You know the mass and need the downward pull of gravity. |
| Support force | For an object at rest on a level surface with no other vertical forces, support force = weight. | A book on a table, a person on a scale. |
| Tension | A stretching force along a rope. A rope pulled equally from both ends has a tension equal to ONE end's pull. | Tug-of-war, ropes tied to trees, hanging objects. |
| Rope angle | The flatter the rope (smaller angle above horizontal), the larger the tension needed to hold the same weight. | Hammocks, clotheslines, hanging signs. |
| Right-angle forces: R = √(a² + b²) | The resultant of two perpendicular forces (the Pythagorean theorem). | Two forces at 90° to each other. |
| Tip-to-tail rule | Draw each force starting where the last one ended. If the arrows return to the start, the net force is zero. | Showing that forces balance on a diagram. |

**Motion (Chapter 3)**

| Tool | What it says | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average speed = distance ÷ time | How fast, with no direction. | You know how far and how long. |
| d = v × t | Distance at a steady speed. | Speed is constant, or you are using an average speed or average velocity. |
| v ≈ Δx ÷ Δt | Velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time. | You have two position readings close together in time, or the slope of a position-time graph. |
| a = Δv ÷ Δt | Acceleration = (final velocity − starting velocity) ÷ time taken. Units m/s². | You know two velocities and the time between them, or the slope of a velocity-time graph. |
| v = v₀ + a × t | Velocity after time t. If the object starts from rest, v₀ = 0 and this is just v = a × t. | Constant acceleration and you want the speed at a certain time. |
| v\_avg = (v₀ + v) ÷ 2 | Average velocity when acceleration is constant. | Constant acceleration and you want distance without the next formula. |
| d = ½ × a × t² | Distance covered from rest at constant acceleration. | Starting from rest and you know a and t. |
| Free fall | a = g = 10 m/s² downward. Dropped from rest: v = g × t and d = ½ × g × t² = 5 × t². | Only gravity acts (ignore air resistance), going up, down, or at the top. |
| Toss straight up | Time up = v₀ ÷ g. Total time in air = 2 × time up. Return speed = launch speed. Max height = distance fallen in the time up. | A ball thrown up and coming back to the same level. |
| Adding velocities | Ground velocity = object's velocity + medium's velocity. Same direction: add. Opposite: subtract. Perpendicular: R = √(a² + b²). | Boats in currents, planes in wind, walking on moving trains. |

**Reading graphs**

| Feature | On a position-time graph | On a velocity-time graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Height of the line | Where the object is | How fast and which way it moves |
| Slope of the line | **Velocity** | **Acceleration** |
| Flat (horizontal) line | At rest | Constant velocity, acceleration = 0 |
| Straight sloped line | Constant velocity | Constant acceleration |
| Slope up / slope down | Moving in the positive / negative direction | Speeding up / slowing down in the positive direction |
| Line crosses zero | Object passes the origin | Object turns around (velocity changes sign) |

**Falling objects from rest (g = 10 m/s²)**

| Time (s) | Speed (m/s) | Total distance fallen (m) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 10 | 5 |
| 2 | 20 | 20 |
| 3 | 30 | 45 |
| 4 | 40 | 80 |
| 5 | 50 | 125 |

## Part A1: Inertia and Newton's first law

**Big idea.** Objects keep doing what they are already doing unless a net force changes it. An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line. This tendency is called **inertia**. Inertia is a property of matter, not a force, and an object with more mass has more inertia.

This was a big change in thinking. Aristotle taught that moving objects need a continual push to keep moving. Galileo, using ramps and rolling balls, realized that things slow down because of **friction**, a force, and not because stopping is their "natural" state. Remove friction and a moving object just keeps going.

**Watch out:** "No net force" does not mean "no motion." It means *no change* in motion.

**Inertia in everyday life**

- Yank a tablecloth out from under dishes and the dishes stay put. They were at rest, and the quick tug gave them almost no push.
- You are standing on a bus that turns left, and you lurch to the right. Your body was moving straight ahead and keeps trying to. The bus turned out from under you.
- Toss a coin straight up on a train moving at constant velocity and it lands in your hand. The coin shares the train's forward motion and nothing pushes it forward or backward.
- Toss the coin while the train speeds up and it lands *behind* you. The coin keeps its old forward velocity while the train moves ahead.

**Worked example.** A seagull flies in a straight line at a constant 10 m/s and lets go of a clam over the rocks, hoping the fall will crack the shell. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is the clam moving horizontally just before it hits the rocks?

1. Before the gull let go, the clam moved forward at 10 m/s along with the gull.
2. Once released, gravity pulls the clam down, but nothing pushes it forward or backward.
3. No horizontal force means no change in horizontal velocity. The answer is **10 m/s**. Seen from the ground, the clam keeps moving forward as it falls, so it lands well ahead of the spot directly below where it was released. Seen from the gull, which keeps flying at the same velocity, the clam stays directly below the bird the whole way down.

**Try it**

**A1.1** If no external forces act on a moving object, it will

- A) continue moving at the same speed in a straight line.
- B) slow down gradually until it stops.
- C) stop abruptly.
- D) speed up.

**A1.2** A rock drifts through deep space at 20 m/s, far from any planet. What force is needed to keep it moving at 20 m/s?

- A) A force equal to its weight
- B) 20 N
- C) No force at all
- D) It depends on the rock's mass

**A1.3** You whirl a rock on a string in a horizontal circle, and the string suddenly breaks. Seen from above, the rock then moves

- A) in a circle, as before.
- B) in a straight line in the direction it was moving at the moment the string broke.
- C) in a straight line directly away from the center of the circle.
- D) toward the center of the circle.

**A1.4** Which has more inertia, a bowling ball or a tennis ball? How do you know?

**A1.5** A hockey puck slides across ice and slowly comes to a stop. Explain *why* it stops, and explain what would happen on perfectly frictionless ice.

**A1.6** A coin is tossed straight up inside a train moving at constant velocity. Explain why the coin lands back in your hand. Then explain where it lands if the train speeds up while the coin is in the air.

## Part A2: Force as a vector and finding net force

**Big idea.** A force is a push or pull, measured in **newtons (N)**. A force is a **vector**, meaning it has both a **magnitude** (how strong) and a **direction** (which way). You need both to describe what a force does.

When several forces act on an object, what matters is the **net force**, the single combined force. Whether the velocity changes depends on the net force:

- **Net force = 0:** the velocity does not change.
- **Net force ≠ 0:** the velocity changes. The speed can change, the direction can change, or both.

**How to find net force along a line**

1. Pick a positive direction (for example right is +, left is −; up is +, down is −).
2. Add the forces, using the signs.
3. The sign of the answer tells you the direction. The size is the magnitude.

Forces at right angles to each other do **not** cancel. Handle each direction on its own: left-right forces with left-right forces, up-down forces with up-down forces.

**Worked example 1.** A block is pulled 5 N to the left and 15 N to the right. Right is positive:

```latex
\text{net} = (+15) + (-5) = +10 \text{ N}
```

The net force is **10 N to the right**.

**Worked example 2.** An object feels 120 N to the left, 70 N to the right, 45 N up, and 45 N down.

- Up-down: +45 − 45 = 0 N, so these cancel.
- Left-right: +70 − 120 = −50 N.

The net force is **50 N to the left**.

**Try it**

**A2.1** A tree stump is pulled north by a 10 N force and south by a 25 N force. What is the net force (magnitude and direction)?

**A2.2** A box is pushed 30 N to the right, another 20 N to the right, and 10 N to the left. What is the net force?

**A2.3** An object has these forces on it: 100 N up, 60 N down, 35 N left, and 35 N right. What is the net force?

**A2.4** True or false, with a reason: "If the net force on an object is zero, the object must be at rest."

**A2.5** Why is force called a *vector* quantity?

**A2.6** Two 10 N forces act on a box. Describe the directions of the two forces that would make the net force (a) 20 N and (b) 0 N.

**A2.7** ★ A cart is moving to the right. A net force of 8 N points to the *left*. Without any calculation, describe what happens to the cart's velocity over the next few seconds.

## Part A3: Equilibrium

**Big idea.** An object is in **equilibrium** when the net force on it is zero. There are two kinds, and both have balanced forces:

- **Static equilibrium:** the object is at rest.
- **Dynamic equilibrium:** the object moves at constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line).

```latex
\Sigma F = 0
```

**Watch out:** Many people think "it is moving, so there must be a net force." That is Aristotle's idea, and Galileo showed it is wrong. Constant velocity means zero net force. Only a *change* in velocity needs a net force.

A falling insect that reaches a steady speed is a good example. Gravity pulls it down with its weight, and air resistance pushes up with an equal force. The forces balance, so the speed stops changing.

**Finding an unknown force.** If an object is in equilibrium, the known forces and the unknown force must add to zero. So the unknown force is equal in size and opposite in direction to the sum of the known forces.

**Worked example.** Three horizontal forces act on an object in static equilibrium. Two of them are 80 N to the right and 30 N to the left, and the third is unknown. Find the unknown force.

1. Right is positive. The known forces add to +80 − 30 = +50 N, which is 50 N to the right.
2. For zero net force, the unknown force must cancel that: it is **50 N to the left**.
3. Check: +80 − 30 − 50 = 0.

**Try it**

**A3.1** A book sits motionless on a table. Which best describes it?

- A) Static equilibrium
- B) Dynamic equilibrium
- C) Not in equilibrium, because gravity pulls it down
- D) No forces act on it

**A3.2** A hockey puck glides at constant velocity across smooth ice. Is it in equilibrium? If so, which kind? What is the net force on it?

**A3.3** An object is in static equilibrium. Three horizontal forces act on it: 120 N to the right, 45 N to the left, and an unknown force. Find the magnitude and direction of the unknown force.

**A3.4** A parachutist who weighs 600 N falls at a constant velocity. What is the net force on her? What is the air resistance, including its direction?

**A3.5** A car drives at a steady 25 m/s on a straight, level road. The engine pushes the car forward with 2000 N. What is the total friction and air resistance on the car, and what kind of equilibrium is this?

**A3.6** A friend says, "The box is sliding across the floor, so there must be a net force on it." Explain whether your friend is right.

**A3.7** ★ An object has these forces on it: 50 N up, 50 N down, 30 N left, and 30 N right. A classmate says it must be at rest. What is wrong with that claim?

## Part A4: Support force, tension, and force diagrams

**Big idea.** Four forces show up again and again, and a **force diagram** is how you keep track of them. The diagram shows the object as a dot, with an arrow for each force acting on it. Arrow length is proportional to the force's size, and each arrow is labeled.

| Force | What it is | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Weight** | Gravity's pull on the object. W = m × g, with m in kg and g = 10 N/kg. | Always down |
| **Support (normal) force** | The push of a surface on the object. | Perpendicular to the surface, away from it |
| **Tension** | A stretching pull along a rope or string. | Along the rope, away from the object |
| **Friction** | A force from a surface that resists sliding. | Opposite to the motion (or the attempted motion) |

**Key facts**

- A book at rest on a table has a support force equal to its weight, so the two cancel.
- A scale reads the support force. If you stand on two scales, the two readings **add up** to your weight.
- Tension is a force that stretches. If two people pull on opposite ends of a rope with 400 N each and nothing moves, the net force on the rope is **0 N** and the tension is **400 N**, not 800 N. Tension equals one end's pull.
- If a scaffold hangs from ropes at rest, the tensions in the ropes **add up** to the total weight of the scaffold plus the people on it.

**Tip-to-tail check.** If an object is in equilibrium, the force arrows drawn tip-to-tail form a closed shape that comes back to the starting point. If the shape does not close, there is a net force.

**Worked example.** A sled moves at constant velocity as a person pulls it with a rope that points up and to the right. The forces are:

- Weight: 400 N, down.
- Support force: 350 N, up.
- Tension: 130 N along the rope. Its horizontal part is 120 N to the right and its vertical part is 50 N up.
- Friction: 120 N, to the left.

Show that the sled is in dynamic equilibrium.

1. **Vertical forces:** 350 N up + 50 N up (from the rope) = 400 N up, which balances the 400 N weight down. Net vertical force = 0.
2. **Horizontal forces:** 120 N right (from the rope) balances 120 N left (friction). Net horizontal force = 0.
3. Tip-to-tail: start at a point, go down 400, up 350, then along the rope (right 120, up 50), then left 120. You are back at the start, so the forces balance.
4. Net force = 0 and the sled moves at constant velocity, so it is in **dynamic equilibrium**.

**Try it**

**A4.1** A 10 N book rests on a table. What is the support force on it?

**A4.2** A 30 kg dog is sleeping on the floor. What is its weight, and what is the support force on it?

**A4.3** A 500 N student stands at rest on two bathroom scales, with her weight shared equally. What does each scale read?

**A4.4** Two painters with a combined weight of 1300 N stand on a scaffold that weighs 400 N. The scaffold hangs at rest from two ropes. What do the two rope tensions add up to?

**A4.5** In a tug-of-war that is perfectly balanced, each team pulls on the rope with 300 N. What is the net force on the rope? What is the tension in the rope?

**A4.6** A crate is pulled across the floor at constant velocity by a rope. The forces are: weight 800 N down, support force 650 N up, and tension whose horizontal part is 240 N to the right and whose vertical part is 150 N up. (a) What is the friction force? (b) Show that the vertical forces balance.

**A4.7** A person weighs themself on a bathroom scale, then rises up onto their tiptoes and stays still. Does the scale reading change? Explain using equilibrium.

**A4.8** ★ In the worked example above, the person pulls harder and the sled's speed starts increasing. What does that tell you about the horizontal forces?

## Part A5: Angles and tension, and forces at right angles

**Big idea, part 1: rope angles.** When an object hangs at rest from two ropes, the **upward parts** of the two tensions have to add up to the object's weight. Each rope only contributes the part of its pull that points up.

- If both ropes are **vertical**, all of each tension points up. Each rope carries **half the weight**.
- If the ropes are **tilted** away from vertical, only part of each tension points up, so each rope must pull harder. Each tension is **more than half the weight**.
- The **flatter** the ropes (the smaller the angle above horizontal), the less each rope's pull points up, and the **larger the tension** has to be.

Tension depends on the **angle** of the ropes, not on their length. If both ropes make equal angles, the two tensions are equal. If the angles are different, the tensions are different.

**Hammock example.** A hammock hangs between two trees. When the trees are far apart, the ropes are nearly flat, the angle of elevation is small, and the tension is large. When the trees are closer together, the ropes tilt more steeply, the angle is larger, and the tension is smaller.

| Ropes | Angle above horizontal | Tension in each rope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight up (vertical) | 90° | Smallest: half the weight |
| Tilted | Medium | Greater than half the weight |
| Nearly flat | Small | Very large |
| Perfectly flat | 0° | Impossible, because no part of the pull points up |

**Big idea, part 2: forces at right angles.** Two forces that point in perpendicular directions do not simply add. Their resultant is the hypotenuse of a right triangle:

```latex
R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}
```

The same formula works for velocities at right angles (Part B7). Useful sets of numbers: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-8-10, and two equal forces at right angles give about 1.4 times one force (10 N right and 10 N up give about 14 N right-up).

**Worked example.** A 40 N force pulls an object east and a 30 N force pulls it north at the same time. What is the net force?

1. The forces are at right angles, so use the Pythagorean theorem.
2. R = √(40² + 30²) = √(1600 + 900) = √2500 = **50 N**.
3. The direction is between east and north, tilted a bit more toward east, since the east force is larger.

**Try it**

**A5.1** A monkey hangs from the middle of a horizontal rope. The tension in the rope is greatest when the rope

- A) sags a lot.
- B) sags very little.
- C) has the same tension no matter how much it sags.

**A5.2** An 800 N object hangs at rest from two ropes that are both vertical. What is the tension in each rope?

**A5.3** The same 800 N object is now hung from two ropes that are tilted away from vertical, at equal angles. Is the tension in each rope less than, equal to, or greater than 400 N? Explain.

**A5.4** You move the two trees holding a hammock farther apart, but the hammock sags to the same spot. What happens to the angle of the ropes and to the tension in them?

**A5.5** A 6 N force pulls an object east and an 8 N force pulls it north. What is the magnitude of the net force?

**A5.6** Two 10 N forces act on a box at right angles. Is the net force closer to 10 N, 14 N, or 20 N?

**A5.7** A 5 N force pulls a cart east while a 12 N force pulls it north. Find the net force magnitude.

**A5.8** ★ A person tries to pull a clothesline completely flat and horizontal while a heavy shirt hangs from its middle. Use what you know about the upward parts of the tensions to explain why this can never be done.

## Part B1: Speed, velocity, and relative motion

**Big idea.** **Speed** tells you how fast something moves. **Velocity** tells you how fast *and* in which direction, so velocity is a vector and speed is not. Both are measured in units such as m/s or km/h.

```latex
\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} \qquad\qquad d = v \times t
```

- **Average speed** covers a whole trip: total distance divided by total time.
- **Instantaneous speed** is the speed at one moment. A car's speedometer reads instantaneous speed.
- A velocity of +5 m/s and a velocity of −5 m/s have the same speed but opposite directions.

**Relative motion.** Speeds are always measured relative to something. When something moves on top of something else that is also moving, the velocities combine:

- Moving in the **same** direction: **add** the speeds.
- Moving in **opposite** directions: **subtract** the speeds.

**Worked example 1.** A horse gallops 10 km in 30 minutes. Convert 30 minutes to 0.5 hours:

```latex
\text{average speed} = \frac{10 \text{ km}}{0.5 \text{ h}} = 20 \text{ km/h}
```

**Worked example 2.** Jake runs at 4 m/s along a train flatcar that moves at 10 m/s. Relative to the ground:

- Running in the same direction as the train: 10 + 4 = **14 m/s**.
- Running in the opposite direction: 10 − 4 = **6 m/s**.

**Try it**

**B1.1** A car's speedometer shows how fast the car is going at one moment. Is that average speed or instantaneous speed?

**B1.2** A runner covers 400 m in 80 s. What is her average speed?

**B1.3** A cyclist averages 6 m/s for 2 minutes. How far does the cyclist travel? (Convert the time to seconds first.)

**B1.4** A car travels 60 km in 45 minutes. What is its average speed in km/h?

**B1.5** Which of these are vectors: speed, velocity, distance, acceleration?

**B1.6** Katelyn runs along the aisle of a train moving at 8 m/s. Her speed relative to the floor of the train is 3 m/s. What could her speed be relative to the ground? Give both possibilities and say when each happens.

**B1.7** A mosquito flies at 3 m/s straight into a 3 m/s breeze that blows in the opposite direction. What is the mosquito's speed relative to the ground?

**B1.8** A car drives around a circular track at a constant 20 m/s. Is its *speed* constant? Is its *velocity* constant? Explain.

## Part B2: Position-time graphs

**Big idea.** A position-time graph shows **where** an object is at each moment. The **slope** of the graph is the object's **velocity**:

```latex
v = \text{slope} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}
```

- A **steeper** line means a **faster** object.
- A line sloping **up** means motion in the **positive** direction. A line sloping **down** means motion in the **negative** direction.
- A **flat** (horizontal) line means the object is **at rest**, because its position is not changing.

**Watch out:** A position-time graph is not a picture of the path. A flat line does not mean "moving at a constant speed". It means *not moving*. Also, a line that is high on the graph just means the object is far from the origin, not that it moves fast.

**Figure 1** shows a student walking back and forth along a straight hallway. Position is measured from the doorway (x = 0), and positive positions are toward the east end of the hall.

&#91;embedded content: Practice data written for this packet; each dot is a corner of the graph at whole-number values\]

**Worked example.** Find the student's velocity from t = 0 to t = 4 s in Figure 1.

1. At t = 0 the position is 0 m. At t = 4 s the position is 8 m.
2. Slope = rise ÷ run = (8 − 0) ÷ (4 − 0) = 8 ÷ 4 = **+2 m/s**.
3. The sign is positive, so the student is walking toward the east end at 2 m/s.

The straight line means the velocity is constant during that interval. To find the velocity at t = 2 s, you do not need a new calculation: it is the same, +2 m/s.

## Part B3: Velocity from data tables, and acceleration

**Big idea.** **Acceleration** is how quickly velocity changes. Any change in velocity counts: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. Acceleration is a vector and its units are m/s² (meters per second, every second).

```latex
a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_{\text{final}} - v_{\text{start}}}{\Delta t}
```

- **Positive a** with positive velocity: speeding up. **Negative a** with positive velocity: slowing down. A negative acceleration is also called a *deceleration* when the object is slowing down.
- **Zero a** means the velocity is constant. A car at a steady 100 m/s has a = 0.
- Going around a curve at constant speed is still an acceleration, because the *direction* of the velocity changes.

**Getting velocity from a table of positions.** Velocity is change in position divided by change in time:

```latex
v \approx \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
```

If two position readings are close together in time, this gives the velocity at the **midpoint** time between them. To estimate acceleration, find velocity at two different times, then divide the change in velocity by the time between those two midpoints.

**Worked example.** A runner's position is recorded:

| Time (s) | 10 | 12 | 50 | 52 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Position (m) | 30 | 42 | 330 | 348 |

1. Velocity at t = 11 s: Δx/Δt = (42 − 30) ÷ (12 − 10) = 12 ÷ 2 = **6 m/s**.
2. Velocity at t = 51 s: (348 − 330) ÷ (52 − 50) = 18 ÷ 2 = **9 m/s**.
3. Acceleration from t = 11 s to t = 51 s: (9 − 6) ÷ (51 − 11) = 3 ÷ 40 = **0.075 m/s²**.

**Worked example (braking).** A car at 30 m/s brakes at −10 m/s².

- Time to stop: t = Δv ÷ a = (0 − 30) ÷ (−10) = **3 s**.
- Distance: use average velocity. The speed falls steadily from 30 to 0, so v\_avg = (30 + 0) ÷ 2 = 15 m/s, and d = 15 × 3 = **45 m**.

**Try it**

## Part B4: Velocity-time graphs

**Big idea.** A velocity-time graph shows **how fast and in which direction** an object moves at each moment. The **height** of the line is the velocity, and the **slope** of the line is the **acceleration**:

```latex
a = \text{slope} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}
```

- A **flat** line means **constant velocity** and zero acceleration. The object is at rest only if the flat line is at v = 0.
- A line **sloping up** means positive acceleration. A line **sloping down** means negative acceleration.
- Where the line **crosses zero**, the object stops for an instant and **turns around**.
- The object **speeds up** when the line moves **away** from the zero axis, and **slows down** when the line moves **toward** the zero axis. In other words, it speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and slows down when they have opposite signs.

**Watch out:** Compare this with Part B2. On a position-time graph a flat line means *at rest*. On a velocity-time graph a flat line means *constant velocity*. The same-looking line means something different, so always check which graph you are reading.

**Figure 2** shows a cyclist on a straight road. East is the positive direction.

&#91;embedded content: Practice data written for this packet; each dot is a corner of the graph at whole-number values\]

**Worked example.** Find the cyclist's acceleration from t = 0 to t = 2 s in Figure 2.

1. At t = 0 the velocity is 0. At t = 2 s the velocity is +6 m/s.
2. Slope = rise ÷ run = (6 − 0) ÷ (2 − 0) = **+3 m/s²**.
3. Velocity and acceleration are both positive, so the cyclist is speeding up toward the east.

## Part B5: Constant acceleration equations

**Big idea.** When acceleration is **constant**, velocity changes by the **same amount every second**. That makes it possible to predict the speed and the distance covered at any time. Rearranging a = Δv ÷ Δt gives the speed equation, and the distance equations come from using the average velocity.

```latex
v = v_0 + a\,t \qquad\qquad v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2} \qquad\qquad d = v_{\text{avg}}\,t
```

If the object **starts from rest**, then v₀ = 0 and the equations simplify:

```latex
v = a\,t \qquad\qquad d = \tfrac{1}{2}\,a\,t^2
```

**Which equation do I use?**

| You know... | You want... | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a and t, starting from rest | Final speed | v = a × t |
| a and t, starting from rest | Distance | d = ½ × a × t² |
| v and a, starting from rest | Time | t = v ÷ a |
| a, t, and a starting speed v₀ | Final speed | v = v₀ + a × t |
| Starting and final speeds, and t | Distance | d = ((v₀ + v) ÷ 2) × t |

**Watch out:** Do not use d = v\_final × t. The object was slower earlier in the trip, so the distance is smaller than that. Use the *average* velocity, or use ½at².

**Worked example.** A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s².

1. Speed after 3 s: v = at = 2 × 3 = **6 m/s**.
2. Distance in 3 s: d = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = **9 m**.
3. Check with the average: v\_avg = (0 + 6) ÷ 2 = 3 m/s, and d = 3 × 3 = 9 m. ✓
4. Time to reach 30 m/s: t = v ÷ a = 30 ÷ 2 = **15 s**.

## Part B6: Free fall and tosses

**Big idea.** An object is in **free fall** when gravity is the only force acting on it (we ignore air resistance). Free fall is a special case of constant acceleration, with a = g ≈ **10 m/s² downward**. Five facts cover most questions:

1. The acceleration is **the same for every object**, heavy or light.
2. It is the same going **down, going up, and at the very top**. While rising, an object loses 10 m/s of speed every second. While falling, it gains 10 m/s every second.
3. At the **top** of a toss, the velocity is momentarily zero but the acceleration is still 10 m/s² downward. (If the acceleration were zero at the top, the ball would hang there.)
4. A ball thrown straight up **returns with the same speed** it was launched with, and the trip up takes **as long** as the trip down.
5. Each second a falling object covers a **greater** distance than the second before, since it is speeding up.

```latex
v = g\,t \qquad\qquad d = \tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t^2 = 5\,t^2 \qquad\qquad \text{(dropped from rest)}
```

For an object thrown **upward** with starting speed v₀, up is easiest to treat with the symmetry rules:

```latex
t_{\text{up}} = \frac{v_0}{g} \qquad\qquad t_{\text{total}} = 2\,t_{\text{up}} \qquad\qquad h_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t_{\text{up}}^2
```

(The maximum height is the distance an object would fall from rest in the time it takes to rise.) You can also use v = v₀ − g × t, where a positive velocity means upward.

**Worked example 1: dropped object.** A stone falls from rest down a mineshaft and hits the bottom after 4 s.

- Speed at the bottom: v = gt = 10 × 4 = **40 m/s**.
- Depth: d = ½gt² = 5 × 4² = 5 × 16 = **80 m**.

**Worked example 2: a toss.** A ball is tossed straight up at 30 m/s.

1. Time to rise: t = v₀ ÷ g = 30 ÷ 10 = **3 s**.
2. Total time in the air: 2 × 3 = **6 s**, and it lands at **30 m/s** downward.
3. Maximum height: ½ × 10 × 3² = **45 m**.
4. Velocity after 1 s: v = 30 − 10 × 1 = **+20 m/s** (up). After 3 s: **0** (the top). After 4 s: 30 − 40 = **−10 m/s** (10 m/s downward).

## Part B7: Adding velocity vectors

**Big idea.** Velocity is a vector, so velocities combine like forces do. An object's velocity **relative to the ground** is its velocity relative to the water or air **plus** the velocity of the water or air.

```latex
\vec{v}_{\text{ground}} = \vec{v}_{\text{in the medium}} + \vec{v}_{\text{medium}}
```

There are three cases:

| Case | Example | How to combine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same direction | Plane with a tailwind | Add the speeds |
| Opposite directions | Plane flying into a headwind | Subtract the speeds; the direction is that of the larger one |
| Right angles | Boat pointed straight across a river current, plane in a crosswind | R = √(a² + b²) |

**Drawing the vector diagram (tip-to-tail).**

1. Draw the first velocity as an arrow, with its length proportional to its speed.
2. Start the second arrow at the **tip** of the first.
3. Draw the resultant from the **tail of the first** arrow to the **tip of the last**.
4. Label each arrow with its speed and direction.

For right angles, the three arrows form a right triangle, and the resultant is its hypotenuse. The resultant always points partly in the direction of the current or wind. That is why a boat pointed straight across a river drifts downstream.

**Worked example.** A boat moves at 6 m/s relative to the water, in a river that flows east at 2 m/s. Find the boat's velocity relative to the ground in each case.

- **Boat points east (with the current):** 6 + 2 = **8 m/s east**.
- **Boat points west (against the current):** 6 − 2 = **4 m/s west**, since the boat's speed is the larger one.
- **Boat points north (across the current):** the velocities are at right angles, so R = √(6² + 2²) = √40 ≈ **6.3 m/s**, directed mostly north but tilted east.

## Part C: Putting it together

Chapters 2 and 3 tell one story: **a net force changes velocity, and acceleration is how we measure that change.** The table below collects the connections that show up most often on tests.

| If you see... | Then... | So the net force is... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Constant velocity (flat line on a v-t graph, straight line on an x-t graph) | a = 0 | Zero (equilibrium) |
| Speed changing, direction changing, or both | a ≠ 0 | Not zero |
| Free fall (only gravity acts) | a = 10 m/s² down | Equal to the weight, pointing down |
| Constant speed around a circle | Direction keeps changing, so a ≠ 0 | Not zero, pointing toward the center |
| Two perpendicular forces or velocities | Pythagorean theorem for either | Resultant = √(a² + b²) |

**Worked example.** A ball is tossed straight up. At the very top of its path, its velocity is zero for an instant. Is the ball in equilibrium at that moment?

No. Gravity still pulls it down with a force equal to its weight, and nothing balances that force. The net force is not zero, so the velocity is changing (from upward to downward) and the acceleration is 10 m/s² downward. A velocity of zero for an instant is not the same as having zero net force.

**Connecting questions**

## Answer key

Check your work against these answers after you try each question. If your answer differs, find the step where your thinking went a different way.

**Part A1: Inertia**

- **A1.1** A.
- **A1.2** C. No force is needed to keep an object moving at constant velocity.
- **A1.3** B. The rock moves in a straight line in the direction it was moving when the string broke.
- **A1.4** The bowling ball. It has more mass, so it has more inertia and is harder to start, stop, or turn.
- **A1.5** Friction (and a little air resistance) pushes backward on the puck, so there is a net force that slows it. On frictionless ice there would be no net force, and the puck would slide at constant velocity forever.
- **A1.6** The coin shares the train's forward velocity, and nothing pushes it forward or backward, so it keeps that velocity and lands in your hand. If the train speeds up, the coin keeps its old forward velocity while the train moves ahead, so it lands behind you.

**Part A2: Net force**

- **A2.1** 25 − 10 = 15 N toward the south.
- **A2.2** 30 + 20 − 10 = 40 N to the right.
- **A2.3** Up-down: 100 − 60 = 40 N up. Left-right: 35 − 35 = 0. Net force is 40 N up.
- **A2.4** False. Zero net force means the velocity does not change, so the object could be at rest or moving at constant velocity.
- **A2.5** The effect of a force depends on both how strong it is and which way it points. Two forces with the same magnitude but different directions have different effects.
- **A2.6** (a) Both forces point in the same direction. (b) The forces point in opposite directions.
- **A2.7** The cart slows down. If the net force kept acting, it would stop and then speed up toward the left.

**Part A3: Equilibrium**

- **A3.1** A (static equilibrium).
- **A3.2** Yes, dynamic equilibrium, because its velocity is constant. The net force is 0 N.
- **A3.3** The known forces add to +120 − 45 = 75 N to the right, so the unknown force is **75 N to the left**.
- **A3.4** The net force is 0 N. Air resistance is **600 N upward**, equal to her weight.
- **A3.5** **2000 N backward**, equal and opposite to the engine force. It is dynamic equilibrium.
- **A3.6** Not necessarily. If the box slides at constant velocity, the net force is zero (the push balances friction). A net force is needed only if the box's velocity is changing.
- **A3.7** The net force is zero in both directions, so the object is in equilibrium. But equilibrium includes constant-velocity motion, so it could be at rest or moving at constant velocity.

**Part A4: Support force, tension, force diagrams**

- **A4.1** 10 N, upward.
- **A4.2** Weight = 30 × 10 = 300 N. Support force = 300 N, upward.
- **A4.3** 250 N on each scale.
- **A4.4** 1300 + 400 = 1700 N.
- **A4.5** Net force on the rope is 0 N. Tension is 300 N.
- **A4.6** (a) Friction is 240 N to the left, to balance the 240 N rightward part of the tension. (b) Up: 650 + 150 = 800 N, which equals the 800 N weight down.
- **A4.7** No. The person is still at rest, so the support force still equals the weight.
- **A4.8** The forward part of the tension is now greater than the friction force, so there is a net force forward and the sled is not in equilibrium.

**Part A5: Angles, tension, right-angle forces**

- **A5.1** B. The flatter the rope, the greater the tension.
- **A5.2** 400 N each.
- **A5.3** Greater than 400 N. Only part of each tension points upward, so each rope has to pull harder for the upward parts to add up to 800 N.
- **A5.4** The ropes become flatter, so the angle gets smaller and the tension gets larger.
- **A5.5** √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 N. (The 6-8-10 triangle.)
- **A5.6** About 14 N.
- **A5.7** √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 N.
- **A5.8** A perfectly flat rope would have tension pointing only sideways, with no upward part to support the shirt's weight. The tension would have to be infinite, so the rope always sags.

**Part B1: Speed, velocity, relative motion**

- **B1.1** Instantaneous speed.
- **B1.2** 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s.
- **B1.3** 2 min = 120 s, so d = 6 × 120 = 720 m.
- **B1.4** 45 min = 0.75 h, so 60 ÷ 0.75 = 80 km/h.
- **B1.5** Velocity and acceleration.
- **B1.6** 11 m/s if she runs in the same direction as the train, or 5 m/s if she runs in the opposite direction.
- **B1.7** 0 m/s.
- **B1.8** The speed is constant, but the velocity is not, because the direction keeps changing.

**Part B2: Position-time graph (Figure 1)**

- **B2.1** 8 m.
- **B2.2** 0 m (the doorway).
- **B2.3** 0 m/s (flat line, so at rest).
- **B2.4** Slope = (−8 − 8) ÷ (12 − 8) = −16 ÷ 4 = **−4 m/s**: 4 m/s in the negative direction (toward the west end).
- **B2.5** Slope from 16 s to 20 s = (−4 − (−8)) ÷ 4 = **+1 m/s**.
- **B2.6** From 4 s to 8 s and from 12 s to 16 s.
- **B2.7** From 0 s to 10 s (after the start).
- **B2.8** From 0 s to 4 s and from 16 s to 20 s.
- **B2.9** From 8 s to 12 s, at 4 m/s (the steepest line).
- **B2.10** No. The position is zero at that instant, but the slope is −4 m/s, so the student is moving.
- **B2.11** Distance = 8 + 16 + 4 = **28 m** (the total length of the walk). The final position is **−4 m**, which is 4 m toward the west end from the doorway. Distance adds up every step, while position only says where the student ended up.

**Part B3: Tables and acceleration**

- **B3.1** (a) (32 − 20) ÷ 2 = 6 m/s. (b) (140 − 120) ÷ 2 = 10 m/s. (c) (10 − 6) ÷ (15 − 5) = 0.4 m/s².
- **B3.2** 60 ÷ 10 = 6 m/s².
- **B3.3** 0 m/s², because the velocity is constant.
- **B3.4** (4 − 12) ÷ 4 = **−2 m/s²**. The negative sign means velocity is decreasing: the cyclist is slowing down while moving in the positive direction.
- **B3.5** 0 m/s². It moves 8 m every second, which is a constant velocity of 8 m/s.
- **B3.6** (a) t = (0 − 30) ÷ (−10) = **3 s**. (b) d = 15 × 3 = **45 m**. (c) a = (0 − 30) ÷ 0.05 = **−600 m/s²**, which is 60 times the braking acceleration.
- **B3.7** Yes. Its velocity changes because the direction changes, even though the speed does not.
- **B3.8** a = (−6 − 6) ÷ 0.2 = **−60 m/s²**.

**Part B4: Velocity-time graph (Figure 2)**

- **B4.1** +6 m/s (6 m/s east).
- **B4.2** −4 m/s (4 m/s west).
- **B4.3** 0 m/s² (flat line).
- **B4.4** Slope from 6 s to 8 s = (0 − 6) ÷ 2 = **−3 m/s²**.
- **B4.5** (−4 − 0) ÷ 2 = **−2 m/s²**.
- **B4.6** (0 − (−4)) ÷ 2 = **+2 m/s²**.

- **B4.8** From 0 s to 8 s (velocity is positive).

- **B4.10** Average velocity = (0 + 6) ÷ 2 = 3 m/s, so d = 3 × 2 = **6 m**.
- **B4.11** A flat line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity (+6 m/s east), not rest. The cyclist is stopped only where the line is at zero.
- **B4.12** The velocity is negative (moving west) and the acceleration is negative too. When they have the same sign, the speed increases. On the graph, the line moves farther from zero.

- **B5.1** 2 m/s².
- **B5.2** (a) v = 2 × 3 = 6 m/s. (b) d = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 m.
- **B5.3** v = 3 × 5 = **15 m/s**. d = ½ × 3 × 5² = **37.5 m**.
- **B5.4** t = v ÷ a = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 **s**.
- **B5.5** v = 50 × 60 = **3000 m/s**.
- **B5.6** v = 5 × 4 = 20 m/s. d = ½ × 5 × 4² = 40 m. With averages: v\_avg = (0 + 20) ÷ 2 = 10 m/s, and d = 10 × 4 = 40 m. Both agree.
- **B5.7** v = 20 + 3 × 4 = **32 m/s**.
- **B5.8** The student used the final speed for the whole trip, but the car was slower earlier. The average speed is (0 + 15) ÷ 2 = 7.5 m/s, so d = 7.5 × 5 = **37.5 m**.

- **B6.1** C (acceleration).
- **B6.2** v = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s. d = 5 × 3² = 45 m.
- **B6.3** d = 5 × 6² = 5 × 36 = 180 m.
- **B6.4** 5 = 5t², so t = 1 s. v = 10 × 1 = 10 m/s.
- **B6.5** v = 20 × 5 = 100 m/s. d = ½ × 20 × 5² = 250 m.
- **B6.6** (a) +10 m/s (10 m/s up). (b) 0 m/s (the top). (c) −10 m/s (10 m/s down). (d) 4 s. (e) 10 m/s² downward. (f) ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m.
- **B6.7** After 1 s: v = 5 − 10 = −5, so **5 m/s downward** (the rock rose for half a second, then started falling). After 2 s: v = 5 − 20 = −15, so **15 m/s downward**.
- **B6.8** It must rise for 3 s, so v₀ = 10 × 3 = **30 m/s**.
- **B6.9** Both hit with the same speed. The ball thrown up rises, stops, and comes back down past the cliff edge with the same speed it was thrown with, going downward. From there it is exactly like the ball thrown down.
- **B6.10** She rises for 0.5 s, so h = 5 × 0.5² = **1.25 m**.
- **B6.11** It is a straight line sloping downward with slope −10 m/s². It starts at +20 m/s at t = 0, crosses zero at t = 2 s (the top of the path), and ends at −20 m/s at t = 4 s.

**Part B7: Adding velocity vectors**

- **B7.1** 90 km/h.
- **B7.2** 70 km/h.
- **B7.3** √(100² + 100²) ≈ **141 km/h**.
- **B7.4** √(80² + 60²) = **100 km/h**.
- **B7.5** (a) 100 m ÷ 1 m/s = 100 s. (b) 1 m/s × 100 s = 100 m south. (c) Speed = √(1² + 1²) ≈ 1.4 m/s, and the distance traveled is about 1.4 × 100 ≈ 141 m.
- **B7.6** (a) 2 + 1.5 = **3.5 m/s east**. (b) 2 − 1.5 = **0.5 m/s west**. (c) √(2² + 1.5²) = √6.25 = **2.5 m/s**, toward the north and tilted east.
- **B7.7** Point the boat **upstream**. The upstream part of the boat's velocity cancels the current, so the resultant points straight across. In the tip-to-tail diagram, the boat's arrow is angled upstream, the current's arrow points downstream from its tip, and the resultant goes straight across.

**Part C: Connecting questions**

- **C1** (a) 0 m/s². (b) 0 N. (c) 0.02 N upward.
- **C2** (a) No, the direction changes. (b) Yes. (c) No. The net force points toward the center of the circle.
- **C3** (a) 0 m/s. (b) 10 m/s² downward. (c) No, because the weight is not balanced.
- **C4** The net force is zero (dynamic equilibrium). The forward pull on the sled equals the backward friction force.
- **C5** (a) The tension equals the weight. (b) The position-time graph is a straight line sloping upward (slope 3 m/s). The velocity-time graph is a flat line at +3 m/s.
- **C6** (a) √(30² + 40²) = 50 N. (b) √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s. (c) Both combine two perpendicular vectors, so both use the Pythagorean theorem.
- **C7** (a) 0 N. (b) 0 m/s². (c) The velocity-time graph is a flat line at 5 m/s. The position-time graph is a straight line sloping upward with slope 5 m/s. (d) 5 × 4 = 20 m.
- **C8** (a) The net force equals the rock's weight, pointing down, so the acceleration is 10 m/s² downward. (b) Air resistance has grown until it equals the weight. The net force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the rock is in dynamic equilibrium.
